entries.title: Zakat is an obligation
entries.statement: Zakat is the obligatory yearly payment from wealth that reaches a minimum amount (nisab) and has been held for a lunar year. It is one of the five pillars of Islam.

basis.arabic: وَأَقِيمُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتُوا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَٱرْكَعُوا۟ مَعَ ٱلرَّٰكِعِينَ
basis.translation: Establish worship, pay the poor-due, and bow your heads with those who bow (in worship).

basis.arabic: خُذْ مِنْ أَمْوَٰلِهِمْ صَدَقَةً تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِم بِهَا وَصَلِّ عَلَيْهِمْ ۖ إِنَّ صَلَوٰتَكَ سَكَنٌ لَّهُمْ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ
basis.translation: Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow, and pray for them. Lo! thy prayer is an assuagement for them. Allah is Hearer, Knower.

basis.arabic: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ أَنفِقُوا۟ مِن طَيِّبَـٰتِ مَا كَسَبْتُمْ وَمِمَّآ أَخْرَجْنَا لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ ۖ وَلَا تَيَمَّمُوا۟ ٱلْخَبِيثَ مِنْهُ تُنفِقُونَ وَلَسْتُم بِـَٔاخِذِيهِ إِلَّآ أَن تُغْمِضُوا۟ فِيهِ ۚ وَٱعْلَمُوٓا۟ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌ
basis.translation: O ye who believe! Spend of the good things which ye have earned, and of that which We bring forth from the earth for you, and seek not the bad (with intent) to spend thereof (in charity) when ye would not take it for yourselves save with disdain; and know that Allah is Absolute, Owner of Praise.

basis.paraphrase: The Prophet, sending Mu'adh to Yemen, told him to teach that Allah made zakat obligatory on their property, taken from the wealthy among them and given to the poor among them.
basis.chapterHeading: Obligatory Charity Tax (Zakat): The obligation of Zakat

entries.title: Who may receive zakat
entries.statement: The Quran names eight categories who may receive zakat: the poor, the needy, those who collect it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing captives, debtors, the cause of Allah, and the wayfarer.

basis.arabic: ۞ إِنَّمَا ٱلصَّدَقَـٰتُ لِلْفُقَرَآءِ وَٱلْمَسَـٰكِينِ وَٱلْعَـٰمِلِينَ عَلَيْهَا وَٱلْمُؤَلَّفَةِ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَفِى ٱلرِّقَابِ وَٱلْغَـٰرِمِينَ وَفِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱبْنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ ۖ فَرِيضَةً مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ
basis.translation: The alms are only for the poor and the needy, and those who collect them, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and to free the captives and the debtors, and for the cause of Allah, and (for) the wayfarer; a duty imposed by Allah. Allah is Knower, Wise.

basis.paraphrase: Zakat is taken from the wealthy of a community and returned to its poor.

entries.title: The rate is 1/40 (2.5%)
entries.statement: On zakatable money and precious metals above the nisab, zakat is one fortieth, which is 2.5%.

basis.paraphrase: In Abu Bakr's written instructions on zakat, silver is zakatable at one fortieth (the sunnah.com English text adds '2.5%'), and nothing is due if it is under 200 dirhams.
Five dirhams are due on 200 dirhams, and half a dinar on 20 dinars, after a year; more is reckoned proportionally. (Half of 20 is one fortieth.)
Ibn 'Umar and 'A'ishah: the Prophet took half a dinar from every twenty dinars or more.

notes: Rate is recorded as 1/40 = 0.025 for the engine.

Every source opened here for the rate speaks of gold and silver. Applying 1/40 to cash and trade goods is how the fatwa bodies cited in this record state it (for example Jordan's General Iftaa' Department 3712 concludes that 2.5% of the total is paid on a merchant's trade goods, cash and collectible debts); it is not repeated as a separate basis.

entries.title: One lunar year (hawl)
entries.statement: Zakat on money and precious metals is due after the wealth has been held for one full lunar year while at or above the nisab.

basis.paraphrase: Zakat is payable on 200 dirhams (or 20 dinars) once a year has passed on them. The report adds that no zakat is due on property until a year has passed; the narrator says he is unsure whether part of the wording is 'Ali's own or the Prophet's, and a later note says the sub-narrator Ibn Wahb added the 'year' sentence as from the Prophet.
'A'ishah heard the Prophet say there is no zakat on wealth until a year (hawl) has passed.

positions.label: Count the whole amount at the yearly date, including money added during the year

attribution.who: Fatwa Center at Islamweb

positions.summary: Pay zakat on the entire amount whether it increased or decreased during the year; what matters is that the nisab is met, even if one gets more money after the lunar year began.

positions.label: Count only what has been held for the full lunar year

attribution.who: Fatwa Center at Islamweb

positions.summary: Zakat is due on the amount in the bank account that reached the nisab and stayed a full lunar year; an amount that reached the nisab but has not been held a full year is not due before then, unless it is profit from the amount already held a year. Paying in advance on the newer amount is permitted.

entries.title: Nisab: the textual basis
entries.statement: The narrations set the minimum at 20 dinars (mithqal) of gold and 200 dirhams of silver; below this there is no zakat on that metal.

basis.paraphrase: 200 dirhams of silver, and 20 dinars of gold, held for a year.
No zakat is due on less than five awaq of silver (the sunnah.com English note equates this to 200 dirhams).
No zakat on less than five camels, five ounces (awqiyah) of silver or five wasqs of produce.

entries.title: Nisab: modern conversions to grams
entries.statement: Published conversions of the textual nisab into grams differ. The record lists them with where each is published and does not choose.

positions.label: 85 g gold, 595 g silver

attribution.who: Fatwa Center at Islamweb

positions.summary: 20 mithqal = 85 g of pure gold (1 mithqal = 4.25 g); 200 dirhams = 595 g of pure silver.

positions.label: 85 g gold, 595 g silver

attribution.who: Mufti of Federal Territory's Department, Malaysia

positions.summary: Nisab of money 'is 20 mithqal of gold (85 grams) or 200 dirhams of silver (595 grams)'.

positions.label: 85 g gold (from a 4.25 g dinar)

attribution.who: General Iftaa' Department, Jordan

positions.summary: Says 85 g is the view of most modern scholars and the one adopted by the Department; the fatwa gives no silver weight.

positions.label: 85 g of 21-carat gold, at market price

attribution.who: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta

positions.summary: Defines the nisab as 85 grams of 21 carat gold according to market price. The 21-carat wording appears in fatwas 7705, 6759 and 6754 and does not appear in fatwa 7746.

positions.label: 85 g gold (no carat stated)

attribution.who: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta

positions.summary: Gives the nisab as '85 grams of gold' (twice) without naming a carat.

positions.label: 85 g of 24-karat gold

attribution.who: General Iftaa' Department, Jordan

positions.summary: 'The equivalent of 85 grams of 24-karat gold' for a merchant's zakat threshold.

positions.label: 87.47 g gold, 612.35 g silver

attribution.who: Darul Ifta Birmingham

positions.summary: 612.35 grams of silver or 87.47 grams of gold or currency equivalent to that amount, citing Radd al-Muhtar vol. 2 p. 5.

positions.label: 96 g gold (from a 4.8 g dinar)

attribution.who: General Iftaa' Department, Jordan, reporting a view used in a Shafi'i textbook

positions.summary: Reports that those who estimate the old dinar at 4.8 g reach 96 g, 'the Nisaab adopted in the Shafie book Al-Fiqh al-Manhaji'; the Department itself adopts 85 g.

entries.title: Difference: gold and silver jewellery worn for personal use
entries.statement: Scholars differ on whether permitted jewellery that is worn is zakatable. Jewellery kept as savings and not worn is treated as zakatable in the sources opened.

basis.paraphrase: A woman came with her daughter wearing two heavy gold bangles; the Prophet asked if she paid zakat on them and warned about bangles of fire; she took them off and gave them for Allah and His Apostle.
basis.chapterHeading: On The Meaning Of Kanz (Treasure) And Zakat On Jewellery

basis.paraphrase: Two women with gold bracelets were asked if they had paid their zakat and told to pay it.
basis.chapterHeading: What Has Been Related About Zakat On Jewelry

basis.paraphrase: 'A'ishah was asked by the Prophet whether she paid zakat on two silver rings she had made; he said it was enough to take her to the fire.
basis.chapterHeading: On The Meaning Of Kanz (Treasure) And Zakat On Jewellery

positions.label: Zakatable at nisab, whether worn or not

attribution.who: Hanafi school, as stated by the Mufti of the Federal Territory

positions.summary: 'Madhhab Abu Hanifah states that zakah is obligatory when the nisab is sufficient, whether the nisab is on its own or if other property is combined with it.'

positions.label: Not zakatable if worn and permitted

attribution.who: Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools, as stated by the Mufti of the Federal Territory

positions.summary: 'for permissible adornments that are used and worn, then zakat is not obligatory on them.' The office says this is the opinion it is inclined to.

positions.label: Not zakatable if worn and permitted

attribution.who: General Iftaa' Department, Jordan (Shafi'i; says Maliki and Hanbali agree)

positions.summary: Not obligatory on permissible jewellery used as a woman's ornament even at the nisab; 'the stronger opinion of our Madhab (Shafie)', also adopted by Maliki and Hanbali, citing Mughni al-Muhtaj 2/95, Hashiyat al-Dasuqi 1/490 and Kashshaf al-Qina' 2/234; reports Malik's Muwatta' on 'A'ishah and Ibn 'Umar.

positions.label: No zakat on women's jewellery

attribution.who: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta

positions.summary: 'A woman's jewelry is not zakatable.' (Also fatwa 6759: 'There is no zakat on women's jewelry.')

positions.label: Jewellery kept for saving, or not worn, is zakatable at nisab and hawl

attribution.who: General Iftaa' Department, Jordan; Mufti of the Federal Territory

positions.summary: If the jewellery is meant for hoarding it is liable once it reaches the nisab and a lunar year passes; An-Nawawi (Al-Majmu' 5/519) is quoted for the majority view. Fatwa JO-3712 adds that adornment gold is exempt 'unless it exceeds the customary amount'. MY-38 treats unworn, stored jewellery as zakatable.

entries.title: Difference: debts you owe
entries.statement: Scholars differ on whether the debts you owe reduce the wealth on which zakat is calculated.

positions.label: Deduct debts you owe

attribution.who: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta

positions.summary: If the outstanding instalments are in your name, deduct all remaining instalments and pay zakat on what remains if it reaches the nisab and is surplus to basic needs. (Note: this fatwa also deducts instalments not yet due.)

positions.label: Deduct debts you owe, unless you have surplus assets that could pay them

attribution.who: Fatwa Center at Islamweb, quoting Ibn Qudamah

positions.summary: Permissible to deduct a mortgage debt from the wealth at nisab if you have no surplus assets that could settle it; if surplus assets cover only part, deduct the rest. Quotes Ibn Qudamah: debt prevents zakat only when it consumes the nisab or leaves less than the nisab.

positions.label: Deduct liabilities, after basic needs

attribution.who: Darul Ifta Birmingham (citing Radd al-Muhtar)

positions.summary: Nisab is for wealth over and above basic needs and free from debts; if after deduction of liabilities the amount exceeds the nisab, zakat is due.

positions.label: Do not deduct debts you owe

attribution.who: General Iftaa' Department, Jordan (Shafi'i reasoning), in a merchant's case

positions.summary: 'Debts owed by the merchant do not affect zakat liability'; the fatwa reasons that zakat is tied to the actual wealth while debt is a liability, and that the zakat texts are general. Tax liabilities unpaid at year end are likewise not deducted.

entries.title: Difference: money owed to you
entries.statement: Money owed to you by a debtor who can and will pay is treated as your wealth. Scholars differ on money from a debtor who is unlikely to pay or who delays.

positions.label: Count it each year if the debtor is able to pay on request

attribution.who: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta; General Iftaa' Department, Jordan
attribution.locator: Answer, second paragraph; JO-3712 'As for debts owed to the merchant'

positions.summary: Zakat becomes due at the end of each hawl even if the creditor has not collected, because it is wealth held by another. Egypt adds it counts with the creditor's other money towards the nisab.

positions.label: Doubtful or delayed debt: pay for all past years when you recover it

attribution.who: Shafi'i school, as stated by Egypt's Dar al-Ifta and Jordan's General Iftaa' Department

positions.summary: Egypt: 'the position of Shafi'i scholars and is the stricter opinion.' Jordan: 'zakat is due for all the past years when the debt is finally recovered. This is more cautious.'

positions.label: Doubtful or delayed debt: pay for one year when you recover it

attribution.who: Hanafi school, as stated by Egypt's Dar al-Ifta

positions.summary: 'Hanafi scholars maintained that zakat is due on such a loan for a hawl when the creditor regains its possession and this is more facilitating.'

positions.label: Doubtful or delayed debt: pay for one year when you recover it (a second statement)

attribution.who: Maliki school, as stated by Jordan's General Iftaa' Department; the same one-year rule is given by the Fatwa Center at Islamweb without naming a school

positions.summary: Jordan quotes Mawahib al-Jalil 2/321: a non-manager pays zakat for one year only when he receives it. Islamweb tells a lender not to pay before receipt and to pay for one year on receipt, with past years being 'safer and more prudent'.

entries.title: Difference: which nisab to use for cash and mixed assets
entries.statement: Gold and silver nisabs differ greatly in value today. The sources differ on whether to measure cash and mixed assets against gold, against the lower of the two, and on whether gold and silver are combined.

positions.label: Use the gold nisab for cash

attribution.who: Fatwa Center at Islamweb

positions.summary: Bank notes: the nisab is 85 g of gold or 595 g of silver, but determining it by gold is preferred because scholars agreed the weight of the mithqal but differed on the dirham.

positions.label: Cash is zakatable at the value of 85 g of gold

attribution.who: Fatwa Center at Islamweb; Egypt's Dar al-Ifta; General Iftaa' Department, Jordan
attribution.locator: IW-81355 Answer, third paragraph; EG-7746 Answer; JO-3712 conclusion

positions.summary: Cash and trade goods are measured against the gold nisab. Islamweb: cash worth 85 g of gold. Egypt (7746): merchandise equal to 85 grams of gold or more. Jordan (3712): the equivalent of 85 grams of 24-karat gold.

positions.label: Use the lower of the gold and silver nisab values

attribution.who: Majority of scholars, as reported by the Fatwa Center at Islamweb

positions.summary: 'the majority of the scholars valued it to the least Nisaab from both [gold and silver]'; a few valued banknotes only to gold.

positions.label: Combine gold and silver to reach either nisab

attribution.who: Majority of scholars, as reported by the Fatwa Center at Islamweb

positions.summary: If neither metal alone reaches its nisab but the value of both combined reaches either nisab, zakat is due.

positions.label: Do not combine gold and silver

attribution.who: Imam al-Shafi'i and others, as reported by the Fatwa Center at Islamweb

positions.summary: Combining should not be done while they are two different kinds and neither has reached a nisab.

entries.title: Zakat al-fitr: who pays, for whom, when
entries.statement: Zakat al-fitr is a small obligatory payment at the end of Ramadan, due on each Muslim and paid before the Eid prayer; the hadith specify it as a sa' of food. Ask your local masjid or zakat committee for this year's amount.

basis.paraphrase: The Prophet made zakat al-fitr (a sa' of dates or barley) obligatory on every Muslim, slave or free, male or female, young or old, and ordered it paid before people went out to the Eid prayer.
Ibn 'Umar gave on behalf of children too, and people used to give a day or two before Eid.
basis.chapterHeading: Sadaqat-ul-Fitr on a slave as well as on a free Muslim

basis.paraphrase: It was prescribed as purification of the fasting person from idle and obscene talk and as food for the poor; if paid before the Eid prayer it is accepted as zakat, and if after it is an ordinary sadaqah.
basis.chapterHeading: Zakat For The Closing Of Fast At The End Of Ramadan

basis.paraphrase: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: a sa' of food was given in the Prophet's time; foods named were barley, raisins, cottage cheese and dates.
basis.chapterHeading: Sadaqat-ul-Fitr is to be given before the 'Eid prayers

sources.title: Paying zakat-ul-fitr in cash or as food products (Fatwa 7732, 23 Feb 2015)

notes: No amounts are recorded anywhere in this record. Use the sentence: "Ask your local masjid or zakat committee for this year's amount."

Conditions stated by the fatwa bodies, not by a hadith opened here: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta (7732) says it is for every person or head of a family who has food in excess of what he needs on the last day of Ramadan; Jordan's article (5786) lists being Muslim, the sunset ending Ramadan, and surplus beyond basic needs, and says whoever supports another also pays for them. These are those bodies' statements.

Timing detail: sunnah.com 1511 reports the Companions' practice of giving a day or two early; the Jordan article gives the due time as the arrival of the night of Eid. The engine need not decide this; the explainer can show the range.
The hadith text uses units (sa') and foods; this record gives no weight conversion, because a gram figure would be a choice and no amounts are recorded.
Whether it is paid as food or as its value is a documented difference, covered in the entry fitr-food-vs-cash; this entry does not settle it.

entries.title: Difference: zakat al-fitr in food or in cash value
entries.statement: Scholars differ on whether zakat al-fitr may be paid as its cash value instead of as food. The positions below are each attributed to their source.

positions.label: Food of the staple diet

attribution.who: Imam al-Shafi'i, as stated by Egypt's Dar al-Ifta; and Jordan's General Iftaa' Department states it

positions.summary: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta states that Imam al-Shafi'i 'contends otherwise' to the permissibility of paying value, because zakat had originally been prescribed in kind. Jordan's General Iftaa' Department states that zakat al-fitr should be given as the staple food of the land.

positions.label: Cash value

attribution.who: Hanafi school, as stated by Egypt's Dar al-Ifta and by Jordan's General Iftaa' Department

positions.summary: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta states that 'It is permissible in our school to pay the equivalent value of wheat', quoting Al-Sarakhsi's Al-Mabsut (vol. 3, pp. 107-8). Jordan's General Iftaa' Department states that Hanafi scholars have permitted giving it as monetary value, considering it more beneficial for the poor and easier for the giver.

positions.label: Cash value where there is need or public benefit

attribution.who: Hanbali scholar Ibn Taymiyya, and a report from Imam Ahmad, as reported by Egypt's Dar al-Ifta

positions.summary: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta reports that the Hanbali scholar Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya (Majmu' al-Fatawa 25/25-83) maintained that paying the value is permissible in cases of need or public benefit, and that a report from Imam Ahmad (cited by Al-Mawardi, Al-Insaf 3/182) holds that giving the value in cash fulfils the obligation.

positions.label: Depends on the food available where the payer lives

attribution.who: Contemporary scholars, as reported by Egypt's Dar al-Ifta

positions.summary: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta reports that where staple food is abundant cash may be better for the poor, and where food is scarce or hard to get it is not acceptable to pay cash; 'The criterion ... is the availability of food, especially staple foodstuff, in abundance.'

Paying zakat-ul-fitr in cash or as food products (Fatwa 7732, 23 Feb 2015)

notes: The calculator does not compute zakat al-fitr. The explainer shows these positions and the sentence: "Ask your local masjid or zakat committee for this year's amount."
JO-4209 also gives an amount for Jordan; it is deliberately not recorded.

Jordan's page (JO-4209) also ranks the options in its own words and makes a statement about all schools; that framing is the Department's and is deliberately not reproduced in this record, which sets the positions out without ranking them.

Left out: a Maliki position on cash fitr (no source opened states one). Hanbali: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta (EG-6417) reports Ibn Taymiyya and a report from Imam Ahmad; recorded as an attributed position above, not as the school's settled view. AAOIFI SS 35: on 2026-11-12 the official English page (cis.aaoifi.com/standards/ss-35-zakah/) showed only an overview of the standard; its full text was not available to open from that page, so no AAOIFI position is used.

examples.note: Cash is measured against the value of 85 g of gold (IW-81355) and zakat is 1/40 (Bukhari 1454). 85 g is a test input, not an endorsement.

ifLowerOfTheTwo.note: Lower of the gold and silver nisab values (IW-120628).

examples.note: Same cash gives different results by choice: gold-only (IW-138743) gives 0; the lower of the two (IW-120628) gives 25. Shows why the app must make the visitor choose. No silver-only row for cash: no opened source applies a silver-only nisab to cash (IW-120628 states a silver nisab only for silver held as silver).
Deduct: EG-6754. Do not deduct: JO-3712. Both are above the 8500 nisab.

A debtor able to pay on request is counted each year (EG-7746 second paragraph); the second row models a lender who counts only on receipt, as in IW-426541. Only the first row is Egypt's rule for an able debtor.
100 g of worn gold: Hanafi-style counts it (MY-38 paragraph 3); the other three schools' view as stated in MY-38 and JO-525 excludes permitted worn jewellery.
